memory_update.text: MRVL should remain on the next-pass watchlist as a custom silicon, optical DSP, silicon photonics, and AI data-center connectivity supplier; official 2026 releases mention robust AI demand and NVIDIA NVLink Fusion participation, but it was excluded here due to the five-candidate limit.

CDNS and ARM are credible second-order candidates for custom AI silicon design enablement: Cadence through certified EDA/IP/3D-IC flows and Arm through Neoverse CSS and AGI CPU positioning. They require separate evidence checks before promotion.

The strongest direct evidence in this node currently clusters around AVGO custom AI accelerator revenue, NVDA merchant accelerator/data-center scale, AMD Instinct ramp, TSM advanced packaging/foundry capacity, and EDA/IP providers enabling more custom ASIC design starts.

This pass did not fully cover semiconductor capital equipment suppliers such as ASML, AMAT, LRCX, KLAC, and Tokyo Electron ADR exposure; those map more cleanly to the foundry capacity expansion sub-node and should be handled in a dedicated equipment pass.

AI revenue disclosure quality is uneven: AVGO and NVDA provide clearer AI/data-center evidence, while SNPS and other EDA/IP suppliers often provide product and ecosystem evidence rather than direct AI revenue attribution.
MRVL should remain in the direct custom-AI-silicon bucket, but future layers must separate custom silicon revenue from optics, switching, and generic data-center semiconductor revenue.

SNPS and CDNS are EDA/design-capacity candidates: they may benefit if the AI accelerator bottleneck includes design slots, verification burden, packaging-aware signoff, and advanced-node IP availability.
AMAT is a capacity-enabling equipment candidate across leading-edge foundry, HBM-related memory, and advanced packaging, with evidence strengthened by 2026 NEXX and AI-memory/packaging announcements.
ASX adds OSAT/advanced-packaging exposure to the node; compare its AI package capacity against TSMC internal advanced packaging and other OSATs in later layers.

ONTO was excluded from the capped candidate list but has unusually relevant HBM4 inspection/metrology evidence. It should be considered in the next pass focused on inspection, metrology, yield, and packaging process control.

Additional US-listed equipment and process-control names to test later: KLAC, LRCX, FORM, TER, MKSI, AEIS, COHR, ENTG, ICHR, UCTT, and ACMR. Their inclusion requires ticker-specific evidence of AI accelerator, advanced-node, HBM, or advanced-packaging revenue exposure.
MRVL should remain in the AI custom ASIC universe, but the dashboard should separate disclosed data-center/custom-silicon evidence from unverified hyperscaler customer assumptions.
ALAB is a high-purity adjacent chokepoint candidate for accelerator-cluster connectivity rather than accelerator compute itself.

EDA and IP vendors such as CDNS/SNPS are design-slot chokepoints: increased custom accelerator tape-outs can raise demand for certified advanced-node, 3D-IC, and signoff flows before foundry capacity is consumed.
Advanced packaging bottlenecks should be tracked through both capacity owners such as AMKR/TSM/Intel Foundry and equipment/process-control suppliers such as ONTO/TER/ACMR.
Next Layer 1B pass should evaluate ATE and HBM/interface-IP names not included due to the five-candidate cap: TER, RMBS, SNPS, ACMR, INTC, and MU.

node: AI accelerators, custom ASICs, and advanced foundry capacity
summary: Combined focused Layer 1B searches: Layer 1B universe expansion for the AI accelerator/custom ASIC/foundry-capacity node identifies five US-listed or US-traded public companies with direct exposure: NVIDIA and AMD as merchant accelerator platform vendors, Broadcom as the clearest custom AI accelerator and AI networking supplier with explicit AI semiconductor revenue disclosure, TSMC as the dominant advanced-node and advanced-packaging manufacturing capacity owner, and Synopsys as an EDA/IP bottleneck enabler for custom AI/HPC silicon design flows. This is research support only, not a trading recommendation. The strongest evidence is from company releases; revenue attribution remains uneven because some companies disclose AI/data-center revenue directly while others describe AI exposure qualitatively. Expanded the US-listed universe around the node beyond merchant GPU leaders into five chokepoint-adjacent areas: custom AI silicon design, EDA/IP for advanced-node and multi-die AI chips, wafer-fab and advanced-packaging equipment, outsourced advanced packaging, and HBM/advanced-packaging inspection/metrology. These names are research candidates, not recommendations. The strongest evidence in this pass is for Marvell, Synopsys, Cadence, Applied Materials, ASE Technology, and Onto Innovation having direct product or capacity linkage to AI accelerator/custom ASIC/foundry-packaging constraints. Candidate list is capped at five, so Onto is captured in evidence and memory as a follow-up coverage gap rather than a candidate.
